history.ask: Diarrhea waking the patient from sleep
Antibiotics or hospital admission in the last 8 weeks

options: Suspicious meal or street food before onset
Frequent raw vegetables or unwashed salads outside home

red_flags: Signs of severe dehydration — hypotension, oliguria, confusion
Severe abdominal pain with distension (toxic megacolon)
Age > 50 with a new change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding
Unintentional weight loss or diarrhea waking the patient at night
Profuse rice-water stools with rapid collapse — cholera pattern, notifiable
exam: Vital signs with temperature and postural blood pressure drop
Assess hydration: skin turgor, mucous membranes, sunken eyes
Weigh the patient and compare with any previous recorded weight
Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, masses, and distension
Digital rectal examination — blood on glove, mass, impaction
Examine the neck and hands: goiter, resting tachycardia, fine tremor
Look for mouth ulcers and finger clubbing
Inspect the perianal region for fistula, fissure, or abscess

investigations.test: Stool exam (microscopy: RBCs, pus cells, ova & parasites)
investigations.why: E. histolytica trophozoites or Giardia cysts rule amebiasis/giardiasis in; pus cells with RBCs point to invasive dysentery or ulcerative colitis rather than watery viral illness
Identifies Shigella/Salmonella when stool is bloody or febrile, and confirms suspected C. difficile after antibiotics where toxin testing is available
Anemia flags ulcerative colitis or colorectal carcinoma; eosinophilia supports parasitic infection; leukocytosis supports invasive bacterial infection
Raised supports inflammatory bowel disease or invasive infection; persistently normal supports IBS or lactose intolerance
Quantifies dehydration and hypokalemia from profuse losses — decides who cannot be worked up as an outpatient
Suppressed TSH rules thyrotoxicosis in when chronic diarrhea comes with weight loss, tremor, or palpitations
Second-line — if chronic bloody diarrhea, age > 50 with changed habit, weight loss, or iron-deficiency anemia: confirms ulcerative colitis or colorectal carcinoma

supports: Suspicious meal or affected household contacts
Unsafe water source or raw vegetables
Gradual onset with lower abdominal tenderness
Antibiotics or hospital admission within 8 weeks
No nocturnal diarrhea, no weight loss, normal exam
Pallor or mouth ulcers on exam
Chronic watery diarrhea with weight loss
Goiter or resting tachycardia on exam
Age > 50 with a recent change in bowel habit
Blood mixed with stool and weight loss
Rectal mass or pallor on exam
Watery stools and bloating clearly triggered by dairy
